title: Joash: Good Start, Bad End
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: Joash was seven years old when he became king; he ruled for forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Gazelle (Zibiah), from Beersheba.
Taught and trained by Jehoiada the priest, Joash did what pleased God throughout Jehoiada's lifetime. Jehoiada picked out two wives for him — he had a family of sons and daughters.

The time came when Joash decided to renovate The Temple of God. He got the priests and Levites together and said, “Go out through the towns of Judah and collect the money due as temple taxes from the people for the annual maintenance of The Temple of God. Do it promptly.” But the Levites didn't do it promptly.

The king called for Jehoiada, the chief priest, and said, “Why haven't you made the Levites bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax imposed by Moses, servant of God, and the congregation of Israel, for the Tent of Covenant?” (wicked Queen Athaliah and her sons had broken into The Temple of God and stolen everything in it for use in Baal worship.)

The king ordered a chest to be made, and it was placed outside, at the entrance to The Temple of God. Then they made a proclamation in Judah and Jerusalem: Bring to God the tax that Moses, servant of God, had imposed on Israel in the wilderness.
People were delighted to do it, and they brought it. They dropped money in the chest until it was full.

Every time the chest was full, the Levites would bring it to the king's officials. Then the king's secretary and the chief priest's appointee would empty the chest and return it to its place. They did this every day until they had a large amount of money. The king and Jehoiada turned the money over to the construction foremen of The Temple of God. Then the foremen hired masons and carpenters to restore The Temple of God. They also hired blacksmiths and workers in bronze to repair The Temple of God. The workers kept at it until they had finished the repair — they restored The Temple of God to its original condition and reinforced it. They returned the rest of the money to the king and Jehoiada, who used it to make furnishings for The Temple of God — vessels for worship services, for Whole-Burnt-Offerings, and for the incense, along with dishes and other things made of gold and silver.

During Jehoiada's lifetime, they continued to offer Whole-Burnt-Offerings at The Temple of God. Jehoiada lived to a ripe old age. He died at 130. They buried him in the City of David with the kings because of all the good he had done for Israel — for God and The Temple.

But after the death of Jehoiada, the leaders of Judah came and bowed down before the king, and the king listened to them. Then they deserted The Temple of God, the God of their ancestors, and worshiped the Asherah groves and idols. And God was angry with Judah and Jerusalem because of their guilt. God sent prophets to call them back to him, and they all preached, but no one paid any attention to them.

Then the Spirit of God moved Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest to speak up: “God's word: Why do you cross God's command? You're going down a dead-end road. You've abandoned God, so he's abandoned you!”

But they conspired against him — and at the king's command, they stoned him to death in the courtyard of The Temple of God. That was the thanks King Joash showed the loyal Jehoiada, the priest who had protected and saved his life. He decided to kill his son. As he was dying, Zechariah called out, “Look at this, God! You take care of this!”

That spring, the Aramean army invaded Judah. They reached Jerusalem and massacred the leaders of the people and sent all the plunder they collected to the king of Damascus. The Aramean army came with a small force, but God gave them a large army as plunder because Judah had abandoned the God of their ancestors. The Arameans had carried out the judgment of God against Joash.

They left Joash badly wounded. Then his servants plotted against him for murdering the son of Jehoiada the priest. They killed him in his bed. They buried him in the City of David, but not in the royal cemetery. The two conspirators were Zabad, whose mother Shimeath was from Ammon, and Jehozabad, whose mother Shimrith was from Moab. The story of his sons, the many prophecies about him, and the account of his restoration of The Temple of God can be found in the The Commentary on the Book of the Kings. Amaziah, his son, became the next king.

title: Amaziah's Pride and Fall
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Jehoaddin from Jerusalem. He lived well, but not wholeheartedly. He was, in short, a little wishy-washy in doing God's will. When he had the kingdom firmly in hand, he executed the servants who had killed his father the king. But he didn't kill their children — he obeyed The Revelation in The Book of Moses, God saying, “Don't kill parents for the sins of the children, don't kill children for the sins of the parents; each person will get his comeuppance.”

Amaziah organized Judah and sorted out Judah and Benjamin by families, under captains of thousands and of hundreds. He took a census: all males twenty years and older, and got a count of 300,000 able-bodied men who could handle a spear and shield. He also hired 100,000 soldiers from Israel at a cost of about four and a half tons of silver.

A holy man showed up and said, “No, O king — don't let the Israelite army into this, because God is not on their side — not with any of the Ephraimites — and will make you fall flat on your face — God doesn't take sides, and he'll put you on the losing side if you go ahead with this!”
Amaziah said to the holy man, “But what about all this money — these tons of silver I have already paid out?” The holy man said, “God's help is worth far more to you than that!”
So Amaziah dismissed the hired soldiers and sent them home. They were furious, and went home in a rage.

But Amaziah was optimistic. He marched his army to the Valley of Salt and killed 10,000 men of Seir. The Judahites took another 10,000 alive and marched them to the top of the Rock and threw them down; they were all dashed to pieces.

But the hired soldiers that Amaziah had sent home — the ones who had been told they were not allowed to go to war with him — went on a rampage, raiding the towns of Judah from Samaria to Beth Horon, killing 3,000 people and carrying off a great deal of loot.

On his return from the defeat of the Edomites, Amaziah brought back the gods of the men of Seir and installed them as his own gods, worshiping them and burning incense to them. That ignited God's anger. God sent a prophet who said, “Why on earth are you praying to these gods who couldn't even save their own people from you?”

The prophet was still speaking when Amaziah interrupted: “Did I ask for your advice? Shut up — before I have you killed!” The prophet, still speaking, said, “No more advice — I can see that God has decided to destroy you, because you have done all this and haven't listened to a word I said.”
After thinking it over, Amaziah, king of Judah, sent a challenge to Jehoash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel: “Come and meet with me — face to face!”

Jehoash, king of Israel, replied to Amaziah, king of Judah: “The thornbush in Lebanon sent word to the cedar in Lebanon: 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' But a wild animal from Lebanon passed by and stepped on the thornbush, crushing it. Just because you've beaten Edom in battle, you're getting all big and high and mighty. Relax, stay home. Why court disaster? Why get yourself and Judah killed?”

But Amaziah wouldn't listen. God had already decided to let Jehoash defeat him — his punishment for worshiping the gods of Edom. So Jehoash, king of Israel, came on. The two of them faced off at Beth Shemesh, in Judah. Judah was thoroughly beaten by Israel — all the soldiers straggled home in defeat.

Jehoash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh. Then he entered Jerusalem, and tore down the Jerusalem wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate — about 600 feet of wall. He looted the gold, silver, and furnishings, everything he found in The Temple of God that had been looked after by Obed-Edom, plus the palace treasuries. Then he took hostages and returned to Samaria.

Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, continued as king for fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. The rest of the life and times of Amaziah from start to finish is written in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Israel and Judah.

From the time Amaziah stopped following God, there was a conspiracy to get rid of him in Jerusalem. He ran away to Lachish, but they tracked him down in Lachish and killed him. They brought his body back on a horse and buried him in the City of David with his ancestors.

title: Uzziah: Pride Before the Fall
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § King Uzziah

The people of Judah then took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. The first thing he did after his father died and was buried was to rebuild Elath and restore it to Judah.

Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother was Jecoliah from Jerusalem. He did well in God's eyes, following the example of his father Amaziah. He continued to seek God in the days of Zechariah, the knowledgeable rabbi who taught him to fear God. And God gave him good success as long as he sought God.

He ventured out and fought the Philistines, breaking down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. He built cities in the area around Ashdod among the Philistines. God helped him in his battles with the Philistines, the Arabs in Gur Baal, and the Meunites. The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah; his reputation spread to the borders of Egypt because he was an extremely powerful king.

Uzziah constructed defense towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle, and fortified them. He also built towers in the desert and dug many wells — he had a lot of cattle in the foothills and the plains. He had workers in the fields and vineyards in the mountains and valleys, because he loved working the soil.

Uzziah had a well-trained army ready to fight, arranged by divisions according to the census taken by the secretary Jeiel and the officer Maaseiah, under the leadership of Hananiah, one of the king's officials. The total number of family leaders drawn up in military formation was 2,600. Under them were 307,000 trained soldiers ready for battle to help the king fight against enemies, with 500 of them on constant alert. Uzziah supplied the entire army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones. In Jerusalem he built machines designed by inventors — on the towers and corners — to shoot arrows and hurl large stones. He became famous far and wide, for he was helped wonderfully until he became powerful.

But then the strength and success went to his head. Arrogant and proud, he defied God. He walked into The Temple of God and took over, burning incense on the incense altar. The priest Azariah, backed up by eighty brave priests of God, tried to prevent him. They said, “Uzziah, you have no business burning incense to God. That is the work of the Aaronite priests, who have been consecrated to do that work. Get out of the Sanctuary! You have no business doing this! This is no way to get God's approval.” Uzziah, already holding the censer and ready to burn the incense, flew into a rage at the priests. While he was shaking with rage, a skin disease broke out on his forehead. Azariah the chief priest and the rest of the priests saw the sores the moment they appeared.

Azariah the chief priest and the other priests saw the sores and grabbed him and rushed him out of there as fast as they could. He was also in a hurry to get out because he knew God had hit him. Uzziah had his skin disease for the rest of his life. He lived in a separate house, banned from The Temple of God. His son Jotham ran the royal palace and the government of the country.

The rest of the history of Uzziah, from start to finish, was written by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz. Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors in a field next to the royal cemetery. This was because he had a skin disease, and people said, “He had a skin disease and can't be buried in the royal cemetery.” His son Jotham became the next king.

title: Jotham's Steady Reign
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He lived well in God's eyes, following the example of his father Uzziah, but he didn't go into The Temple of God the way his father had. The people, meanwhile, kept up their pagan worship.

Jotham built the Upper Gate of The Temple of God and built a great deal of wall on the hill of Ophel. He also built cities in the hill country of Judah and fortresses and defense towers in the forests. He also fought and defeated the king of the Ammonites — that year the Ammonites paid him 3.75 tons of silver, 65,000 bushels of wheat, and 65,000 bushels of barley. They kept paying him the same amount for the next two years. Jotham grew powerful because he was single-minded in his life with God.

The rest of the life and times of Jotham, including his wars and achievements, are all written in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Israel and Judah. He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled for sixteen years in Jerusalem. Jotham died and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz became the next king.

title: Ahaz Sells Out to Assyria
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He didn't live well — he didn't do what pleased God like his ancestor David. He lived just like the kings of Israel. He even had images cast for the worship of Baal. He burned incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, sacrificing his own sons in the fire, following the revolting practices of the nations that God had driven out of the country before the arrival of Israel. He worshiped at the local shrines, partying and offering sacrifices on every hill and under every green tree.

Because of all this, God, the God of his ancestors, handed him over to the king of Aram. He defeated him and took many prisoners, and brought them to Damascus. Also, God handed him over to Pekah son of Remaliah, who killed 120,000 in a single day — all first-class soldiers — because they had abandoned God, the God of their ancestors. Zicri, an Ephraimite soldier, killed the king's son Maaseiah, Azrikam the palace steward, and Elkanah, who was second in command to the king. And the Israelites captured 200,000 of their brothers and sisters — mothers and children — and a huge amount of plunder, and hauled it off to Samaria.

A prophet of God named Oded was in the neighborhood. He met the army when it entered Samaria and said, “Pay attention — God, the God of your ancestors, was angry with Judah and used you to punish them; but you took it too far, and God's anger is now on you. What's more, you are planning to make slaves of the people of Judah and Jerusalem! Don't you realize that you are just as guilty as they are before God? Listen to me — return every last one of these prisoners you took from your brothers! If you don't, you'll feel God's fierce anger.”

Some of their Ephraimite leaders — Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berekiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai — stood up against the returning army and said, “Don't bring the captives here! We've already sinned against God, and now you're adding to our sins and guilt. We've sinned enough, and now God's anger is hot against Israel.”

So the soldiers returned the captives and the plunder to the leaders and the congregation. The men named above got up, took the captives, and from the plunder got clothes for the naked, and gave them all sandals, food and drink, and provided first aid to the injured, putting salve on their wounds. They provided donkeys for the feeble, and escorted them back to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.

At about that time, King Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria asking for personal assistance. The Edomites had come back and given Judah a bad beating, taking off a bunch of captives. Adding to the misery, the Philistines were raiding towns in the foothills and the Negev of Judah. They captured Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco and its villages, Timnah and its villages, and Gimzo and its villages, and settled down there. God's affliction on Judah was because of the leadership of Ahaz king of Israel — he'd gotten the whole country into a moral mess and had turned his back on God. Then, to add insult to injury, Tiglath-Pileser the king of Assyria came to him anyway and put the squeeze on him instead of helping him. Ahaz took treasure from The Temple of God, the royal palace, and the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria as a bribe — but it didn't do any good.

Even when bad things were happening to him, King Ahaz continued to be against God. He offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, the ones who had beaten him in battle. He said, “The gods of the kings of Aram helped them — I'll worship them too and maybe they'll help me.” But they were the ruin of him first, and then of all Israel. Ahaz gathered up the furnishings of The Temple of God and smashed them to pieces. Then he boarded up the doors of The Temple of God and set up his own altars to the gods — one in every corner of Jerusalem. He made sex-and-religion shrines in all the towns of Judah — a shrine in every town! — and burned incense to the popular gods. God's anger was hot against him.

The rest of his life, from start to finish, is written in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Judah and Israel. Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem. But he was not buried in the royal cemetery of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah became the next king.

title: Hezekiah Cleans House
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § Hezekiah

Hezekiah became king when he was twenty-five years old and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah. In God's eyes he lived the way his ancestor David did.

In the first month of the first year of his reign, Hezekiah opened the doors of The Temple of God and repaired them. Then he called the priests and Levites together and said, “Listen to me, Levites! Consecrate yourselves and consecrate The Temple of God, the God of your ancestors — get this junk out of the holy place! Our ancestors went wrong and did evil in the eyes of God. They deserted him and turned their backs on God's house of worship. They shut the doors at the entrance so no one could enter, snuffed out the lamps, stopped burning incense, and quit offering Whole-Burnt-Offerings to the God of Israel. And because of that, God's anger flared up against Judah and Jerusalem. He made them into a doom-demonstration, a horror, something to whistle at — as you can see with your own eyes! Our fathers were killed by the sword, and our sons and daughters and wives were taken off as prisoners, all because of this.

“I have made up my mind to make a covenant with the God of Israel so that his anger will subside. Children, don't drag your feet in this! God has chosen you to take your place before him to serve in conducting and leading worship — this is your life work; make sure you do it and do it well.”

The Levites stood at attention: Mahath son of Amasai, Joel son of Azariah (from the Kohathites); Kish son of Abdi, Azariah son of Jehallelel (from the Merarites); Joah son of Zimmah, Eden son of Joah (from the Gershonites); Shimri and Jeiel, sons of Elizaphan; Zechariah and Mattaniah, sons of Asaph; Jehiel and Shimei of the family of Heman; Shemaiah and Uzziel of the family of Jeduthun. They all got together, consecrated themselves, and started on God's work at the king's orders. First they purified The Temple of God. The priests started from the inside and worked out; they emptied the place of the accumulation of pagan junk — piling it in the courtyard of The Temple of God — and the Levites carted it out to the Kidron Valley. They began the Temple cleaning on the first day of the first month and on the eighth day they reached the porch of God. They went on for another eight days, cleaning and consecrating the inner Temple. On the sixteenth day of the first month they were finished.

They reported to Hezekiah the king: “We have cleaned up The Temple of God, including the Altar of Whole-Burnt-Offering, all its furnishings, the Table of the Bread of the Presence with its furnishings, the valuables that King Ahaz had thrown out during his unbelieving reign — we've restored them and consecrated them, and they're all in place, arranged before the Altar of God.”

Then Hezekiah the king went to work: He got up early the next morning and called together the leaders of the city and went to The Temple of God. They brought with them seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats to sacrifice as an Absolution-Offering for the kingdom, for the Sanctuary, and for Judah. He directed the Aaronite priests to offer the sacrifices on the Altar of God. The priests slaughtered the bulls and then took the blood and sprinkled it on the Altar. Then they slaughtered the rams and sprinkled the blood on the Altar. Then they slaughtered the lambs and sprinkled the blood on the Altar. Finally, they brought the goats up; the king and congregation laid their hands on them. The priests slaughtered them and then offered the blood as an Absolution-Offering on the Altar, atoning for the sin of all Israel — for the king had ordered that the Whole-Burnt-Offering and the Absolution-Offering be for all Israel.

He also set the Levites in The Temple of God with instruments — cymbals, harps, and lyres — following the orders of David, Gad the king's seer, and Nathan the prophet. This was God's command conveyed by his prophets.

The Levites formed the orchestra, playing the instruments of David, while the priests took up the trumpets. Then Hezekiah gave the signal — the Whole-Burnt-Offering was offered on the Altar. As soon as the offering was offered, the song of God began, and the trumpets sounded, with the instruments of David king of Israel accompanying them. Everybody joined in — singing, playing, trumpeting — until the Whole-Burnt-Offering was completed. When the offering of the sacrifices was completed, the king and everyone in attendance bowed down and worshiped. The king and leaders told the Levites to praise God using the psalms of David and Asaph the seer. They praised with joy — a climax of praise — and then bowed down in worship.

Hezekiah then made an offering and said, “Now that you have consecrated yourselves to God, come and bring your sacrifices and Thank-Offerings to The Temple of God.” The congregation brought sacrifices and Thank-Offerings and some volunteered to bring Whole-Burnt-Offerings. They brought seventy bulls, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs for Whole-Burnt-Offerings for God. As a Consecration-Offering they brought six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep. The priests, though, were too few to skin and cut up the Whole-Burnt-Offerings — so their brother Levites came to the rescue and helped them until the work was done — and even helped with the Consecrations-Offerings. The Levites had been more careful to consecrate themselves than the priests had been. There was also a lot of Whole-Burnt-Offering, along with the fat of the Peace-Offerings and the Drink-Offerings that went with the Whole-Burnt-Offerings. So the worship in The Temple of God was re-established.
Hezekiah and the people were overjoyed — what God had done for the people! And it happened in no time at all.

title: The Great Passover Comeback
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § A Passover Celebration

Then Hezekiah invited all of Israel and Judah, with personal letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, to come to The Temple of God in Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover to Israel's God. The king, his officials, and the congregation in Jerusalem had decided to celebrate the Passover in the second month. They hadn't been able to do it in the regular way at the regular time because not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people hadn't been able to get to Jerusalem. The king and the congregation thought this was a good idea, so they issued a proclamation to all Israel — from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north — inviting everyone to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover to Israel's God. It was the first time in a long time that they did it right.

The king gave his couriers military orders. They delivered the king's message everywhere in Israel and Judah. The message: “O Israelites! Come back to God, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that he can return to those who remain, who have escaped the grasp of the kings of Assyria. Don't repeat the sins of your ancestors who turned their backs on God, the God of their ancestors, so that he turned his back on them — you can see the consequences in our ruined cities. Don't be bullheaded as your ancestors were. Clasp God's outstretched hand. Come to his Temple of holy worship, consecrated for all time. Serve God, your God. You'll no longer be in danger of his hot anger. If you come back to God, your captive brothers and sisters will be treated compassionately and allowed to come home. God, your God, is generous and kind; he won't keep turning his back on you if you return to him.”

So the couriers set out, going from city to city through the country of Ephraim and Manasseh, as far as Zebulun. But the people sneered at them and turned up their noses. But not all; some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun were sorry for their sins and made the journey to Jerusalem. It was God's hand that was on Judah, to give them a common purpose, to carry out the king's order and God's order to celebrate the Passover.

A huge crowd came together in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unraised Bread in the second month. First they went to work and got rid of the neighborhood altars in Jerusalem, removed all the incense altars, and threw them into the Kidron Valley. Then, on the fourteenth day of the second month, they slaughtered the Passover lambs. The priests and Levites weren't ready; but now, embarrassed in their laziness, they consecrated themselves and brought Whole-Burnt-Offerings to The Temple of God. Ready now, they stood at their posts as set out in The Revelation of Moses the man of God, and the priests sprinkled the blood they'd received from the Levites.

Many in the congregation hadn't consecrated themselves, and so the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for them and consecrated them to God. There were a lot of people, especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, who had not consecrated themselves, but they ate the Passover anyway — the Passover was not celebrated according to the established rules. But Hezekiah prayed for them: “May God who is good — pardon all those who desire to set their hearts on seeking God, the God of their ancestors, even if they are not consecrated for the holy place.”
And God listened to Hezekiah and healed the people.

The Israelites in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unraised Bread for seven days with great joy. The Levites and priests praised God day after day, filling the air with music. Hezekiah rallied the Levites who were skillful at serving God. They celebrated the feast for seven days, sacrificing Peace-Offerings, and giving thanks to the God of their ancestors.
Then the whole congregation agreed to stay another seven days — they just kept on celebrating for another seven days!

Hezekiah king of Judah gave the congregation a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for the offerings, and the leaders also gave the congregation a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. A great number of priests consecrated themselves. The whole congregation of Judah, the priests, the Levites, the congregation that came from Israel, and the resident aliens from both the country of Israel and the country of Judah, celebrated. It was a great celebration in Jerusalem, unequaled since the days of Solomon son of David king of Israel.
The priests and Levites got up and blessed the people. God heard them — their prayer rose to heaven, to his holy place.

title: Giving That Overflows
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: After the Passover celebration, the Israelites who were there fanned out through the towns of Judah, smashed the stone shrines, chopped down the Asherah groves, and demolished the neighborhood shrines and altars — a clean sweep through Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Then they all went back to their own towns, their own homes.

Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites into divisions, each division with its own work — offering Whole-Burnt-Offerings and Peace-Offerings, serving, giving thanks, and praising in the courtyards of God's Temple.

He also designated his own personal contribution for the Whole-Burnt-Offerings: the morning and evening Whole-Burnt-Offerings, the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the Feast-of-God Whole-Burnt-Offerings — as it is written in God's Revelation.
In addition, he asked the people who lived in Jerusalem to give the portion that belonged to the priests and Levites so that they could devote themselves to The Revelation of God.

As soon as Hezekiah's orders were received, the Israelites responded generously: firstfruits of the grain harvest, new wine, oil, honey — everything they grew in their fields. They brought in a tithe — a tenth of everything, too. The people of Israel and Judah living in the cities of Judah also brought in a tithe of cattle and sheep, and a tithe of the dedicated things that had been consecrated to their God. They piled them in heaps! They started doing this in the third month and didn't finish until the seventh month.

When Hezekiah and his leaders came and saw the extent of the heaps of donations, they praised God and commended the people of Israel. Hezekiah then consulted the priests and Levites on how to handle the abundance of offerings.

Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps of donations, and the chief priest Azariah, of the family of Zadok, answered, “From the moment these people brought their gifts to The Temple of God, we have been eating our fill and running over! Because God has blessed his people, there is a lot left over.”

Hezekiah then ordered storerooms to be prepared in The Temple of God. When they were ready, they brought in all the offerings of tithes and sacred gifts. They put Conaniah the Levite in charge, with his brother Shimei as assistant. They were joined by their colleagues Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismakiah, Mahath, and Benaiah. These were the supervisors under Conaniah and Shimei his brother, as directed by King Hezekiah and Azariah the chief priest in The Temple of God. Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the guard at the East Gate, was in charge of the Freewill-Offerings of God and for distributing the contributions made to God and the consecrated gifts. Faithful assistants under him were Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah. They were to distribute the rations in all the priestly towns to their brothers — young and old, in their various divisions. In addition, they distributed to males thirty years and older — to everyone who entered The Temple of God to carry out their daily duties according to their work and their divisions — the priests enrolled by families and the Levites twenty years and older, by their duties and divisions. The official family tree included everyone — children, wives, sons, daughters — the whole extended family; they had to be consecrated and set apart for holy work.

The Aaronites, the priests who lived out on the pasturelands belonging to the priest-cities, were allotted portions in the fields of their cities. Men were appointed by name to distribute the portions to all the males among the priests and to all who were enrolled among the Levites.

Hezekiah did this throughout all Judah. He did what was good and right and true before his God. Everything he took up, whether in worship of God or in obedience to his law and commandments, he did with all his heart, and he was successful.

title: Sennacherib at the Gates
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § Assyria Attacks Judah
And then, after this exemplary track record, this: Sennacherib king of Assyria came and attacked Judah. He put the fortified cities under siege, determined to take them.

When Hezekiah realized that Sennacherib had come with the intent of attacking Jerusalem, he consulted with his officials and officers; they all agreed that it was best to plug the springs and wells outside the city, and the officers all pitched in. There was a great turnout of people to plug the springs and divert the stream flowing through the country. They said, “Why should the kings of Assyria march in and be furnished with running water?”

Hezekiah also went to work repairing every part of the wall that was damaged, built towers over it, and built another wall outside. He reinforced the defensive rampart (the Millo) of the old City of David. He also built a large number of weapons and shields. He appointed military officers in the army and assembled them in the town square.

He gave them this speech of encouragement: “Be strong! Take courage! Don't be intimidated by the king of Assyria and his troops — there are more of us than there are of them. He only has a bunch of mere men; we have our God to help us and fight for us!” Morale surged. Hezekiah's words put steel in their spines.

Later, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was now attacking Lachish, sent a message to Hezekiah along with his officers, addressing Jerusalem and Hezekiah and everyone in Judah. This is what he said: “This is Sennacherib king of Assyria: 'What makes you think you can hole up in Jerusalem under siege? Hezekiah has talked you into coming to Jerusalem, but he'll lead you to starvation and death! Even Hezekiah claims that God will save us from the king of Assyria. But wasn't it Hezekiah who got rid of all the local shrines and altars, telling everyone in Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship at this one altar, and you must burn incense on this one altar'? Don't you know what I and my ancestors have done to all the countries around here? Has any god of any country around here ever been able to stand up to us? Name one god that I or my ancestors have exterminated that has ever been able to stand against us. So what makes you think that your God can stand up to me? Don't listen to Hezekiah's lies. Don't believe him. No god of any country or kingdom has ever been able to stand up to me or my ancestors. What makes you think your God can stand up to me?'”
Sennacherib's servants said worse things — they scoffed at God, the God of Israel, and at Hezekiah, God's servant.

Sennacherib also wrote letters cursing the God of Israel: “Just as the gods of the peoples of other countries couldn't rescue their people from me, so Hezekiah's god won't be able to save his people from me either.”

The Assyrians then shouted in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall — trying to scare and terrorize them so that they could capture the city. They were contemptuous of the God of Jerusalem, just as they had been contemptuous of the gods of all the peoples around them — mere wood-and-stone idols.

King Hezekiah, joined by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, responded by praying, calling up to heaven. God answered by sending an angel who wiped out everyone in the Assyrian camp, both warriors and officers. Sennacherib was forced to return home in disgrace, tail between his legs. When he went into the temple of his god, his own sons killed him.

God saved Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Sennacherib king of Assyria and from everyone else. And he took good care of them. Because of this, many people brought gifts to Jerusalem to give to God, and also many valuables for King Hezekiah of Judah. Hezekiah ended up very highly honored among all the nations.
Some time later, Hezekiah became deathly sick. He prayed to God, and God answered by giving him a miraculous sign.

But Hezekiah became proud and didn't respond with due gratitude — and God, angry, punished him — and Judah and Jerusalem as well. But then Hezekiah, and Jerusalem with him, repented of his arrogance — and God's anger didn't come down on them during Hezekiah's lifetime.

Hezekiah ended up very wealthy and highly honored. He built treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuables. He built barns for the harvest of grain, wine, and oil, and stalls for all kinds of cattle, and pens for the flocks. He founded royal cities for himself and built up huge stocks of sheep and cattle. God gave him a lot, a lot of wealth. And it was Hezekiah who plugged the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channeled the water to the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah succeeded in everything he did. But when the rulers from Babylon sent emissaries to find out about the miraculous sign that had occurred in the land, God left him on his own to see what he would do; he wanted to test his heart.

The rest of the history of Hezekiah, including his acts of faithful love, is written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Judah and Israel. When Hezekiah died, they buried him in the upper part of the royal cemetery. Everyone in Judah and Jerusalem came to the funeral — they honored him in death. His son Manasseh became the next king.

title: Manasseh's Evil, Then His Turnaround
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § Manasseh King of Judah

Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. In God's eyes he lived an evil life, obedient to the tabooed practices of the nations that God had driven out of the country before the arrival of Israel. He rebuilt the neighborhood sex-and-religion shrines that his father Hezekiah had demolished, erected altars to Baal, put up Asherah poles, and worshiped at the cosmic shrines, courted the whole cosmic zoo. He even built altars to the gods of the cosmos in The Temple of God, the very place that God had set aside for worship. Under the slogan “God's Temple in Jerusalem is the place of worship” he built altars for the gods of the cosmos in both courtyards of The Temple of God. He burned his sons as sacrifices in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. He practiced witchcraft and fortunetelling, and operated with a black cat in his lap — a dabbler in the occult. He did a lot that was evil in God's eyes, and, needless to say, it made God angry.

He put the carved image of the sex goddess Asherah that he had made in God's Temple, the very Temple of which God had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this Temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my Name forever. I will never again make the people of Israel wander off — never evict them from the land I gave to their ancestors — if they are careful to live the way I commanded in the Revelation I gave through Moses.”

But Manasseh led Judah and the citizens of Jerusalem off the beaten path into evil practices — evil, for that matter, worse than the nations God had earlier destroyed. When God spoke to Manasseh and his people about this, they didn't even bother to listen.

Then God directed the leaders of the troops of the king of Assyria to come after Manasseh. They put a hook in his nose, shackles on his feet, and took him off to Babylon. Now that he was in trouble, he went to his knees in prayer asking for help — before the God of his ancestors. As he prayed, God was touched; God listened and brought him back to Jerusalem as king. That convinced Manasseh that God was God.

After that, Manasseh rebuilt the outside wall of the City of David to the west of Gihon in the valley, up to the Fish Gate, and around the Ophel, and made it very high. He put his officers in command of the fortified cities in Judah. He also removed the foreign gods and the idol from The Temple of God, and the altars he had built on The Temple hill and in Jerusalem, dumping them outside the city. He restored the Altar of God and offered Peace-Offerings and Thank-Offerings on it. He ordered Judah to worship the God of Israel. But the people kept on offering sacrifices at the neighborhood shrines, though only to their God.

The rest of the life and times of Manasseh, his prayers to his God, and the messages of the prophets who spoke to him in the name of the God of Israel, is written down in The Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. His prayer and how God was touched by his prayer, including all his sins before he humbled himself, and the places where he built the pagan shrines and installed the Asherah sites and the idols he worshiped before his conversion — this is all described in the records of the prophets.
When Manasseh died, they buried him in the palace garden. His son Amon was the next king.
§ Amon of Judah

Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for two years. In God's eyes he lived an evil life, just like his father Manasseh. Amon worshiped all the idols his father had made and served them. But unlike his father Manasseh, he didn't humble himself before God — Amon only got worse.
The officers in his court plotted against him and killed him in his house. The citizens of the country killed all those who had killed King Amon and made his son Josiah king.

title: Josiah Finds the Lost Book
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § King Josiah
Josiah was eight years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. He behaved well before God, living the way of his ancestor David — no detours, no dead ends.

When he was still a young man — in the eighth year of his reign — he started out on the path to God, the God of David his ancestor. Four years later, in the twelfth year of his reign, he began ridding Judah and Jerusalem of the sex-and-religion shrines, Asherah poles, carved idols, and metal images. He directed the demolition of the Baal altars — the pagan altars and the incense altars that were stacked high above them. He had them smashed, crushed the debris into dust, and scattered it over the graves of the worshipers. He burned the bones of the priests on the same altars they had used when alive. He scrubbed the place clean, Judah and Jerusalem, ritual and moral. Josiah then took the cleanup campaign outward to the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, all the way to Naphtali, with their ruins. He demolished the altars, ground to dust the Asherah poles and the carved idols, smashed the incense altars, and left only dust and rubble. Then he went back to Jerusalem.

One day in the eighteenth year of his reign, after he had cleaned up the country, King Josiah sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city administrator, and Joah son of Joahaz the historian to renovate The Temple of God. First they went to Hilkiah the high priest and turned over to him the money that had been collected in The Temple of God by the Levitical guards at the doors — from Manasseh, Ephraim, and the rest of Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from the citizens of Jerusalem. It was then put into the hands of the foremen managing The Temple of God, who then passed it on to the workers repairing God's Temple — the carpenters, construction workers, and masons — so they could buy the lumber and dressed stone for rebuilding the foundations the kings of Judah had allowed to fall to pieces. The workers were honest and diligent. The supervisors were Jahath and Obadiah, the Merarite Levites, and Zechariah and Meshullam from the Kohathites. The Levites — all of whom were skilled musicians — were in charge of the common laborers and supervised the workers as they went from job to job. The Levites also served as accountants, managers, and security guards.

While they were bringing out the money that had been collected at The Temple of God, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of The Revelation of God taught by Moses. He called out to Shaphan the secretary, “We found the Book of The Revelation of God in The Temple of God!” Hilkiah handed the book to Shaphan. Shaphan took the book to the king and reported, “Your servants are doing what you've asked them to. They've gathered the money at The Temple of God and paid it out to the foremen and the workmen.”
Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book.” Then Shaphan read it out loud to the king.

When the king heard what was written in The Revelation, he tore his clothes in dismay. Then the king ordered Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah one of the king's attendants: “Go and pray to God for me and for those who are left in Israel and Judah — find out what this book says that has just been found. God's anger must be burning furiously against us — our ancestors haven't obeyed a thing written in this book of God, followed none of the instructions directed to us.”

Hilkiah and those picked by the king went to Huldah the prophetess — she was the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath, the son of Hasrah, who was in charge of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter. They asked her what was going on. She replied: “God's word, the God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you here, 'This is God's word: I'm bringing disaster on this place and its people, on everything written in the book that the king of Judah has just read. Because they've deserted me and worshiped at the shrines of other gods — they've made me angry at what they've done. My anger is ignited against this place — it's not going to be put out.'

And also tell the king of Judah who sent you to pray to God: 'This is God's word, the God of Israel: Regarding what you read in that book — because you took seriously the doom I spoke against this place and its people, and because you responded in tears, in repentance and sorrow, and tore your clothes, I'll have mercy on you. That's God's word. I'll take care of you: you'll have a quiet death and be buried in peace. You won't be around to see the doom that I'm going to bring on this place and its people.'” The men took her message back to the king.

The king then sent for all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem. The king went to The Temple of God, and everyone in Judah and Jerusalem, along with the priests and Levites — all the people, young and old — went with him. He read the words of the Book of the Covenant that was found in The Temple of God. The king stood by his pillar and before God solemnly committed himself to the covenant: to follow God believingly and obediently, to follow his instructions, heart and soul, on what to believe and do, to confirm with his life the entire covenant, all that was written in the book.
Then he made everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin commit themselves. And they did — they committed themselves to the covenant of God, the God of their ancestors.

Josiah did a thorough job of cleaning up the place — got rid of all the disgusting idols throughout Israelite territory — and made everyone in Israel worship and serve their God. And they didn't waver from that — they continued to follow God, the God of their ancestors.

title: Josiah's Last Passover
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § Josiah's Passover

Josiah celebrated the Passover to God in Jerusalem. They killed the Passover lambs on the fourteenth day of the first month. He gave the priests their duties and encouraged them to do the work of The Temple of God. He addressed the Levites, the teachers of Israel who had been consecrated to God: “Put the holy Chest in The Temple built by Solomon son of David king of Israel. Don't carry it around on your shoulders — you have no more need to do that. Now take care of The Temple of God and the worship of the people. Organize yourselves by families for your respective responsibilities, following the instructions left by David king of Israel and Solomon his son.

Take your place in the Sanctuary based on your family divisions among your brothers, the laypeople — and the Levites will be grouped in the same way. Kill the Passover lambs, consecrate yourselves, and get everything ready for your brothers so they can do what God commands through Moses.”

Josiah provided the master of ceremonies for the people — 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 bulls from the king's own herds for the Passover sacrifices. The king's officials were just as generous — they gave a hundred bulls, besides the 7,600 lambs and goats, to the priests for the Passover offerings; and Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, leaders in The Temple of God, gave 2,600 lambs and goats and 300 bulls to the priests for the Passover offerings; and Conaniah, Shemaiah and Nethanel his brothers, along with the Levitical chiefs Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, gave 5,000 lambs and goats and 500 bulls to the Levites for the Passover offerings.

The work was done — the priests were in their places and the Levites in their divisions as instructed by the king. They killed the Passover lambs, and the priests sprinkled the blood while the Levites skinned the animals. Then they set aside the Whole-Burnt-Offering for the family groups of the people to offer to God as written in the Book of Moses — and they did the same with the bulls. They roasted the Passover lamb over the fire, following the instructions to the letter. They boiled the holy offerings in pots, kettles, and pans and served them quickly to the people.

Afterward, the Levites got what was due to them and the Aaronite priests — because the priests were busy from morning to night offering the Whole-Burnt-Offerings and the fat. So the Levites served themselves and the priests, the sons of Aaron.

The singers, the sons of Asaph, were all in their places, as David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer had instructed. The guards were at each gate; they didn't leave their posts, because their brother Levites had prepared food for them.

Everything went without a hitch in the worship of God that day — the Passover was celebrated and the Whole-Burnt-Offering was offered on the Altar of God as King Josiah had ordered. The Israelites who were there that day celebrated the Passover and the Feast of Unraised Bread for seven days. The Passover hadn't been celebrated like this since the days of Samuel the prophet. None of the kings of Israel had organized a Passover like the one that Josiah organized — involving all of Judah and Israel, the priests and Levites, and all the people who were there that day. This Passover was celebrated in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign.
Some time later, after Josiah had finished restoring The Temple, Neco king of Egypt marched out to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates River. Josiah went out to fight him.

Neco sent messengers to Josiah: “What do we have against each other, O king of Judah? I haven't come to fight against you today. I'm on my way to fight another nation, and God told me to hurry. Get out of God's way; if you don't, he'll kill you.”

But Josiah was stubborn. He refused to turn back. He disguised himself so that he could fight Neco. He didn't take seriously the words of Neco, which were from God. The two kings met on the plain at Megiddo. The archers shot King Josiah. The king said to his servants, “Get me out of here — I'm badly wounded.”

So his servants took him out of the chariot and laid him in the second chariot. They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there. They buried him in the cemetery of his ancestors. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned the death of Josiah. Jeremiah composed an elegy for Josiah. All the singers and their sons and daughters still sing it to this day, a song of lament over Josiah. It became a tradition in Israel; they are recorded in the Laments.

The rest of the history of Josiah, his faithful acts conforming to The Revelation of God, and the whole story from start to finish, are written in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Israel and Judah. By popular choice, Jehoahaz son of Josiah was made king at Jerusalem, succeeding his father.

title: The Fall and the Promise of Return
note: audited: MSG 2Chronicles 36장 전수 대조 (unit 배지 1:1). 1-12장은 MSG 기준 신규 작성, 13-36장은 재청킹 초벌 + 의미 재감사. 슬랭 6 rule 적용. merge/split은 적용하지 않음.
paragraphs: § The Last Kings

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for three months. The king of Egypt dethroned him and fined the country nearly four tons of silver and seventy-five pounds of gold.
Then Neco king of Egypt made Eliakim, brother of Jehoahaz, king of Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Neco took his brother Jehoahaz and carried him off to Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. In God's eyes he lived an evil life.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon attacked him, bound him in chains, and took him off to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar also took things from The Temple of God to Babylon and put them in his temple in Babylon.

The rest of the life and times of Jehoiakim, the disgusting things he did, the things that were found in his conduct, are written in the Royal Annals of the Kings of Israel and Judah. Jehoiachin his son became the next king.

Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for three months and ten days. In God's eyes he lived an evil life. In the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar ordered him brought to Babylon along with the valuables remaining in The Temple of God. Then he made Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king of Judah and Jerusalem.

Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. As far as God was concerned, he was just one more evil king. He never listened to a thing the prophet Jeremiah said, even though the message came straight from God. Then he compounded his troubles by rebelling against King Nebuchadnezzar, who earlier had made him swear in God's name that he would be loyal. He became set in his own stubborn ways — he never gave God, the God of Israel, a thought.

The evil mindset spread to the leaders and priests and filtered down to the people — they, too, lived an evil life, much like the pagans. They polluted The Temple of God, the place that God had set aside for worship in Jerusalem.

God, the God of their ancestors, repeatedly sent warning messages to them. Out of compassion for his people and his dwelling place, he sent them warning messages through his messengers. But they ridiculed God's messengers, mocked his words, and made fun of his prophets to the point that God's anger erupted and there was no way to put it out. He then directed Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, to come up against them. He killed their young men in their own Sanctuary. He showed no mercy to anyone — young men and virgins, old men and grandmothers. He turned them all over to him.

He also took into Babylon all the furnishings, large and small, of The Temple of God, the treasures of The Temple of God, and those of the king and his officials. They burned down The Temple of God, tore down the walls of Jerusalem, burned all the palaces, and destroyed everything of value. He took into exile those who had escaped the killing, and they became slaves to Nebuchadnezzar and his sons until the Persians came to power.
This is exactly the message of God's word that Jeremiah had preached: the desolate land put to an extended sabbath rest — a seventy-year Sabbath rest making up for all the unkept Sabbaths.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia — this fulfilled the message of God's word preached by Jeremiah — God moved Cyrus king of Persia to issue an official announcement throughout his kingdom; he put it in writing. “This is Cyrus king of Persia's Message: God, the God of the heavens, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has also assigned me to build him a Temple of worship at Jerusalem in Judah. All who belong to God's people are urged to return — and may your God be with you! Move along!”
